text: A developer is building a custom tool that lets Claude query a company's order-status database. During testing, Claude frequently calls the tool with malformed date parameters, causing silent failures that are hard to diagnose. Which change would most directly address this issue?
options: Lower the model's effort setting so tool calls become simpler and more deterministic
Replace the custom tool with a built-in filesystem tool, since built-in tools never produce malformed parameters
Increase the context window limit so Claude has more room to format the tool call correctly
Write a clearer tool description and parameter schema (with `strict: true`), and return structured error results (`is_error: true`) that Claude can interpret and act on
correct_answer: Write a clearer tool description and parameter schema (with `strict: true`), and return structured error results (`is_error: true`) that Claude can interpret and act on
explanation: Tool implementation best practice (D) emphasizes precise tool descriptions (specifying expected formats such as ISO-8601 dates), well-defined parameter schemas with `strict: true`, and informative error handling (`is_error: true` on `tool_result`) so Claude can self-correct. Adjusting effort (A) does not fix schema ambiguity, built-in tools (B) cannot query a custom order-status database, and a larger context window (C) does not address parameter formatting or silent error swallowing.

text: An agent needs to perform a destructive action -- deleting records from a production database -- as part of a multi-step workflow. The team wants to ensure a human reviews and explicitly approves this specific action before it executes, without blocking the rest of the agent's read-only operations. Which tool usage pattern best satisfies this requirement?
options: Configure all read-only and write tools in the agent's toolset to require manual approval before every call
Implement an approval pattern that gates only the destructive tool call, requiring explicit confirmation before execution while allowing read-only tool calls to proceed autonomously
Remove the delete capability entirely and have a human perform all deletions manually outside the workflow
Upgrade the model tier to Opus so the agent is less likely to make mistakes when deleting records autonomously
correct_answer: Implement an approval pattern that gates only the destructive tool call, requiring explicit confirmation before execution while allowing read-only tool calls to proceed autonomously
explanation: Tool usage patterns include selective approval gating (e.g., via `PreToolUse` returning `permissionDecision: "ask"` or human-in-the-loop confirmation) for specific sensitive or destructive actions (B), providing human oversight without sacrificing autonomy on safe read-only operations. Gating every tool call (A) is overly restrictive and hurts efficiency. Removing the capability (C) eliminates the workflow's automation value. Switching model tiers (D) does not provide a deterministic safeguard against destructive actions.

text: A developer is building an MCP server that will run as a local subprocess alongside a desktop Claude application, with no need to support multiple simultaneous remote clients. Which communication pattern is most appropriate for this deployment?
options: A persistent WebSocket connection routed through a cloud-hosted load balancer
A public REST endpoint exposed over the internet with OAuth2 client authentication
`stdio` transport, since the server and client run on the same machine and communicate over standard input/output streams (while logging diagnostics to `stderr`)
A distributed message queue broker to decouple the client and server across data centers
correct_answer: `stdio` transport, since the server and client run on the same machine and communicate over standard input/output streams (while logging diagnostics to `stderr`)
explanation: MCP supports `stdio` and Streamable HTTP transports. `stdio` transport (C) is purpose-built for local, single-client scenarios where a host application (such as Claude Desktop or Claude Code) spawns the MCP server as a local subprocess and exchanges JSON-RPC messages over `stdin`/`stdout` (with logs written only to `stderr`). The other options (A, B, D) introduce unnecessary network complexity and infrastructure for a purely local subprocess.
section: Tools and MCPs - MCP Server Development

text: A team wants to give Claude the ability to search internal engineering wikis, access a set of pre-written document templates on demand, and reuse parameterized prompt snippets across several internal applications -- all through a single, independently maintained service that multiple teams can connect to. Which capability of the Model Context Protocol best matches this combined requirement?
options: An MCP server exposing tools for search, resources for templates, and prompts for the reusable snippets, all maintained centrally
A single custom in-process tool with a very large function schema covering all three needs inside one application
A Claude Skill bundled separately into each individual application repository that needs the functionality
Pasting all wiki articles, templates, and prompt snippets directly into each application's system prompt
correct_answer: An MCP server exposing tools for search, resources for templates, and prompts for the reusable snippets, all maintained centrally
explanation: MCP servers can expose three core primitives -- tools (model-controlled actions like wiki search), resources (app-controlled read-only data like templates), and prompts (user-controlled reusable prompt templates) -- from a single centrally maintained service (A), making it ideal for sharing live integrations across multiple applications. A single oversized in-process tool schema (B) conflates distinct concerns and is not shared across apps, duplicating Skills per application (C) does not provide a shared live wiki search service, and pasting everything into system prompts (D) wastes context and does not stay current.
section: Tools and MCPs - MCP Server Development

text: A developer is deciding how to give Claude the ability to generate properly formatted quarterly financial reports following a fixed internal template, a capability needed only within Claude Code sessions for one internal team, with no need for external system calls. Which approach best fits this use case given the tradeoffs among built-in tools, custom tools, Skills, and MCPs?
options: Build and deploy a remote MCP server since any reusable formatting capability must be hosted as an MCP service
Rely solely on a built-in tool such as `Grep`, since built-in tools can be configured to follow any custom report template
Author a Claude Skill (`SKILL.md`) packaging the template, formatting instructions, and any helper scripts, since it loads on demand and requires no external service calls
Write a custom tool with a function schema that returns the static report template text on every API invocation
correct_answer: Author a Claude Skill (`SKILL.md`) packaging the template, formatting instructions, and any helper scripts, since it loads on demand and requires no external service calls
explanation: Claude Skills (`SKILL.md`) are designed for packaging reusable domain-specific know-how, instructions, templates, and local helper scripts that load on demand when relevant, without requiring an external live service connection (C). Building a full MCP server (A) adds unnecessary operational overhead when no live external system is involved. Built-in tools (B) are for file/shell operations rather than domain templates. A custom function tool (D) is meant for executing external logic, not delivering static procedural instructions.
